about.title: How it works
about.sourceTitle: Where does the data come from?
about.sourceText: The forecast comes from {openMeteo}, which serves the {cams} European air quality model. The model calculates a value for every hour on a grid of squares about 11 km across.
about.modelNote: These are model estimates, not measurements. Next to a busy road or a smoking chimney the air can be worse than the app shows. Smog Radar is general information, not medical advice.
about.eaqiText: The European Air Quality Index (EAQI) rates five pollutants: fine particles PM2.5, particles PM10, nitrogen dioxide, ozone and sulphur dioxide. Each gets its own rating, and the result is the worst of them. That's why the app names the pollutant pushing the number up.
about.eaqiScale: The European Environment Agency (EEA) sorts air into six bands. The numbers are Open-Meteo's scale, which gives each band a range. Sulphur dioxide counts towards the result, but the app doesn't show it separately, since its levels are low across most of Europe.
about.walkTitle: When is it fine to go for a walk?
about.walkBasis: The answer follows the EEA's advice. From “Poor” the EEA suggests most people consider cutting down intense outdoor activity, and sensitive people from “Moderate”.
about.sensitiveNote: Sensitive people include those with asthma or heart and lung conditions, children and older people. You can switch to the stricter thresholds in the settings.
about.windowsTitle: When should I open the windows?
about.windowsBasis: The EEA says nothing about airing rooms, so these thresholds are the app's own. A short airing starts at a lower AQI than the cautious walk answer. Rooms still need fresh air, so for a middling result the app suggests a short airing rather than keeping the windows shut.
about.betterTitle: Where does the better-time tip come from?
about.betterText: If now isn't the best time, the app looks through the forecast for the first time the answer would be the best one. If there is none, it says so. The chart also marks the cleanest {hours} hours in a row. Both only count hours from {from} to {to} local time.
about.mapText: The map is the only part that shows measurements rather than the model: the latest hourly PM2.5 readings from stations across Europe, collected by {openaq}. They include official monitors and low-cost sensors. Readings older than {hours} hours are left out.
about.mapSurface: Between stations the colour is averaged: the closer a station, the more its reading counts. Further than {km} km from the nearest station there is no colour, because nobody measures there. The map covers PM2.5 only, so it can look better than the overall result when, say, ozone is the problem.
about.whoText: The “Pollutants” tab compares each concentration with the {who}. They are health recommendations, not law. They refer to 24-hour averages (8-hour for ozone), while the app shows hourly values, so the comparison is only a rough guide. The walk and window answers use the European index only.
about.privacyIntro: There are no accounts, no analytics and no tracking.
privacy: On your first visit the hosting provider works out your city from your IP address. The app only gets the city's name and rough coordinates, and doesn't store the address.
“Use my location” asks your browser for permission. The position is rounded to about 1 km before it leaves your device.

The forecast, place search (Photon, OpenStreetMap data) and station readings are fetched by the app's server, so those services never see your IP address. The place search gets what you typed and your position to within about 50 km, so nearby places come first.
Your browser loads the map background directly from OpenFreeMap.
Cookies remember your last place, your language and sensitive mode; browser storage remembers the theme.
